A day in the life of a barista
Opening
You arrive before the café opens. The machine warms up, the grinder is set, the first shots are tasted and dialled in. Milk and cups are prepared.

The machine's group heads and steam wands are cleaned, the grinder is emptied and wiped. Everything must be ready for tomorrow morning.

The bar's tools
Espresso machine
Pushes hot water through compacted coffee at about 9 bar of pressure. It is the heart of the bar.
group head = where the water comes out
Grinder
Grinds the beans just before brewing. A fine or coarse setting decides how fast the espresso flows.
grind setting
Portafilter
The basket with a handle that holds the ground coffee. It locks into the machine and the espresso flows out underneath.
basket
Tamper
Presses the coffee in the basket flat and firmly, so the water passes evenly through all of the coffee.
tamping = pressing
Milk jug and steam wand
The steam wand heats and froths milk. Milk is frothed in a stainless steel jug. The wand is wiped immediately after every use.
microfoam
Precision scale
Weighs the coffee and the espresso that flows out. Measuring is the secret to every cup tasting the same.
dose = amount of coffee used
Knock box
After brewing, the portafilter is emptied by knocking it on this box's bar. Coffee grounds are never poured into the sink – they clog the drain.
grounds = used coffee

Make the espresso step by step
The master wants a double-shot espresso. Do the steps in the right order.
Remove the portafilter and run a short flush from the group head
Leftover grounds from the last brew are cleaned away and the machine's temperature stabilises.
Before anything else, you must get the machine ready for the next coffee.
Wipe the basket with a dry cloth
Coffee put into a wet basket won't brew evenly.
The basket must be dry and clean before you add coffee.
Grind the beans fresh (about 18 g for a double shot)
Ground coffee loses its aroma within minutes, so it is ground just before brewing.
The basket is ready; now you need the coffee to put in it.
Distribute the coffee evenly in the basket
If the coffee piles up on one side, water takes the easiest path and the espresso turns sour and watery.
The coffee must be level and even before you press it.
Tamp flat and firmly with the tamper
Compacted coffee resists the water, so the water passes through slowly and evenly.
The coffee is distributed; now it needs to be compacted.
Lock in the portafilter and put the cup underneath
Once the portafilter is locked in, start brewing without much delay, otherwise the coffee burns in the machine.
The coffee is ready; it has to go back into the machine.
Start brewing: about 36 g of espresso in 25–30 seconds
If it flows too fast it is sour, too slow and it is bitter. Time is adjusted with the grind size.
Everything is in place; one last step left.
Info card: A good espresso
Water passes through the coffee at about 9 bar of pressure.
Water temperature is usually 90–96 °C; boiling water burns the coffee.
Double shot: about 36 g of espresso from about 18 g of coffee in 25–30 seconds (1:2 ratio).
The hazel-coloured foam on top is called crema; it is a sign of fresh coffee.
If the flow is too fast, grind finer; if too slow, grind coarser.
Coffee menu
Espresso
The basis of everything. Served in a small cup with crema on top.
single shot / double shot
Americano
Espresso + hot water. For those who want a longer, lighter coffee without milk.

Macchiato
Espresso + a spoonful of milk foam. Italian for "stained". Don't confuse it with the big caramel drink at chain cafés.
espresso + a little foam
Cappuccino
Espresso + hot milk + thick foam. Usually in a 150–180 ml cup.
thick foam
Latte
Espresso + lots of hot milk + thin foam. In a large glass, smooth to drink.
lots of milk, thin foam
Flat white
Espresso + a little milk + very fine, silky foam. Smaller than a latte, with a stronger coffee taste.
microfoam
A cortado
Espresso + roughly the same amount of hot milk, very little foam. Served in a small glass (about 100–130 ml); a strong coffee taste, but softened.
espresso + equal milk

hygiene mistake
Wiping the steam wand with a damp cloth and giving a short purge
Milk dries on the wand within seconds. It is wiped and purged right after every steaming.
Knocking out the puck, wiping the basket and flushing the group head after a shot
Old grounds and coffee oils make the next shot bitter. A short flush cleans the shower screen.
Rinsing the used milk jug
Every drink starts with a clean, cold jug. Leftover milk spoils the taste and foam of fresh milk.
Backflushing with a blind basket and machine detergent
Detergent backflushing is done at the end of the day and always followed by a water rinse. Only on machines with a three-way valve.
Soaking baskets and portafilters in detergent water
Built-up coffee oil only dissolves when soaked. The plastic handle of the portafilter should stay out of the water.
Emptying and wiping the grinder hopper
Beans left in the hopper go stale overnight and their oil sticks to it. The beans go into a sealed container.
Emptying and washing the drip tray
It is emptied whenever it fills during the day and always washed at closing; leftover milk and coffee start to smell.
Re-steaming leftover steamed milk
Reheated milk tastes burnt and won't foam well; lukewarm milk sitting around is also a bacteria risk. Use fresh milk for every drink.
Wiping the counter with the steam wand cloth
Cloths are kept separate: one only for the steam wand, one for the counter, one for the portafilter. Mixing them spreads dirt and milk residue.
Leaving open milk out on the counter
Milk must stay in the cold chain: it goes back into the fridge (0–4 °C) right after use.
Touching a cup rim or lid after handling money without washing hands
Money is one of the dirtiest things there is. Wash your hands after the till; always hold cups by the body or handle.
Clean bar rules
The steam wand is wiped and purged after every steaming.
After every shot the basket is cleaned and the group head flushed.
Cloths are kept separate, milk always stays in the fridge.
Milk is never steamed twice.
Busy morning
8:30 in the morning, the café is full. The master is on a break, the bar is yours.
"My coffee is very sour!" You notice the shot ran in 17 seconds. What do you do?
Grind a bit finer and make a new shot
Correct. Fast flow = under-extracted coffee = sour. A finer grind slows the water down.
Grind coarser
A coarser grind speeds the water up even more, so it gets more sour.
Add sugar on the side and send it out
It hides the problem but doesn't fix it. The customer may not come back.
Make it again with the same setting
The same setting gives the same result.
The new shot ran in 28 seconds. What do you tell the customer?
"Sorry about that, I fixed the setting. Enjoy!"
Admitting the mistake and saying you fixed it builds trust.
"Espresso is always a bit sour anyway."
It makes the customer wrong; the problem was real.
You hand it over without saying anything
The job is done, but the customer doesn't feel looked after.
You frothed milk and there is milk left on the steam wand. 3 orders are waiting.
Wipe it straight away with a damp cloth and purge a short burst of steam
Milk dries and sticks within seconds. Bacteria grow on a wand that's left dirty.
I'll wipe it when the orders are done
Dried milk is a hygiene problem and gives the next milk a burnt taste.
I wipe it with a dry napkin and don't purge
The outside gets clean, but milk stays inside the wand. Purging steam is a must.
An opened milk carton has been sitting on the counter for 40 minutes.
I put it back in the fridge right away
Opened milk stays in the fridge (4 °C or below) and only comes out while in use.
We use it a lot, it can stay out until evening
At room temperature milk spoils quickly; customers' health is put at risk.
I put it next to the machine to keep it warm
A warm spot is where bacteria grow fastest.
Golden rules of the bar
Sour and fast: grind finer; bitter and slow: grind coarser.
Steam wand: wipe and purge a short burst of steam right after every use.
Opened milk goes in the fridge, at 4 °C or below.

Milk and foam
Cold milk, cold jug
The milk should come straight from the fridge. Cold milk gives you more time to add air before it heats up.
start cold
Fill the jug about halfway
Usually just below the base of the jug's spout. There must be room for the foam to rise.
fill line
Clean the wand first
Purge a short burst of steam from the wand so the condensed water inside doesn't get into the milk.
purge
Add air: the hissing sound
The tip sits just below the surface of the milk and you hear a "tsss" like paper tearing. This is done in the first seconds, while the milk is still cold.

Whirlpool
Dip the tip a little deeper so the milk spins in the jug. Big bubbles break and the foam becomes silky and glossy.
microfoam

The coffee's journey
The coffee belt
Coffee grows in hot countries around the Equator, such as Ethiopia, Colombia and Brazil. The soil and altitude affect its taste.
origin
Arabica and Robusta
Arabica is more aromatic and acidic. Robusta is stronger, more bitter and has more caffeine. Blends can use both.
species
Processing method
Washed coffees taste cleaner and brighter; naturally dried (natural) ones are fruitier and sweeter.
washed / natural
Roast
A light roast is fruity and acidic; a dark roast is bitter and full-bodied. For espresso, a medium-dark roast is usually chosen.
roast level
Freshness
Roasted coffee rests for a few days and is then at its best for a few weeks. Check the roast date on the bag.
roast date
Water
Almost all of a cup of coffee is water. Filtered water improves the taste and protects the machine from limescale.
water quality

Make the grind coarser
Make the grind finer

Nothing, it's normal

Latte art: heart
The customer wants a heart on their latte. Do the steps in the right order.
Pour fresh espresso into the cup and swirl the milk until glossy
A pattern only comes out with fresh crema and silky milk.
First, the ingredients must be ready.
Tilt the cup towards you
In a tilted cup the milk spreads more slowly, leaving room for the pattern.
The angle of the cup is set before you start pouring.
Pour a thin stream from high up until the cup is half full
Milk poured from high up dives below the surface, mixes with the coffee and forms the base.
The base must be formed before the pattern.
Bring the jug spout right down to the surface and increase the flow
Milk poured close up stays on the surface and forms a white spot.
For a white pattern, the jug must be close to the surface.
Keep pouring at the same spot until the white circle grows, then level the cup
This circle is the body of the heart.
First the circle that forms the heart's body must appear.
Raise the jug and finish with a thin stream through the middle of the circle
The thin stream cuts the circle in the middle and draws the pointed tip of the heart.
Last step: drawing the tip of the heart.
